 The federal budget promises simpler taxes for Canadians. Here’s what you need to know.
 Susan Kao Toronto star illustration using pexels photo 
 Make us a preferred source on Google 
 By  Lora Grady Personal Finance Reporter 
 Good news for Canadians who dread doing their taxes: the 2026-27 federal budget aims to simplify the filing process.
 The budget, tabled on Nov. 5, says that the measures announced “will reduce the compliance and administrative burden for millions of taxpayers” and will simplify tax filing for more than 1.5 million people.
 The budget doesn’t propose any big tax reductions or incentives, says Jason Heath, certified financial planner and managing director at Objective Financial Partners. It’s mostly related to administrative changes, “which makes taxes a little bit easier going forward.”
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Experts weigh in on five ways proposed tax changes could affect Canadians, from increased benefit payments and flat amounts for deductions and credits to a new filing deadline.
 Boosting benefits
 The budget proposes a one-time supplement to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB) equal to half of the maximum yearly amount, which would be paid out in early 2027. For families, the maximum amount of the supplement would be $223 per adult and $117 per child, and for singles the maximum would be $117.
 The budget also proposes topping up the Canada Workers Benefit (CWB) — a refundable tax credit that supplements earnings of workers with low and modest income — and renaming it the Build Canada Workers Benefit. Singles without children   could get a maximum annual payment of $1,859 (up from $1,709), and families, including couples and single parents, could get $3,143 (up from $2,943).
 Making the Canada Caregiver Credit a refundable tax credit
 Currently, caregivers whose income is too low to pay tax don’t fully benefit from the Canada Caregiver Credit (CCC). That’s because it’s a non-refundable tax credit, which means it can only reduce the amount of taxes you owe. The government proposes making it a refundable credit, which would mean caregivers who don’t owe taxes could actually receive refunds. Eligible caregivers could receive up to $1,260 annually, even if they owe little or no taxes.
 “Individuals who might not have owed taxes but were still paying to support and care for their family members weren’t getting anything back,” says Adam Pegler, senior financial and tax planning adviser at Desjardins. The proposal to make a refundable credit would put money back into their hands, which they could use to support themselves and their family members, he adds.
 The government says this measure would offer support to 180,000 caregivers who don’t currently receive the benefit. If approved, this change would kick in for the 2027 tax year.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Increasing instalment thresholds for tax owing
 Most Canadians pay taxes through withholdings on their employment income that are remitted to the Canada Revenue Agency by their employers. But when people earn income from sources that aren’t subject to withholding (which includes certain sources of pension income, business income and rental income), they may be required to pay income tax in quarterly instalments. Seniors also often get income from sources that don’t automatically withhold taxes (such as a Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF), Old Age Security (OAS), and the Canada Pension Plan (CPP)).
 The budget proposes raising the minimum amount of income tax owing that triggers the obligation to pay tax in instalments to $7,500 from $3,000 (where it was set in 2008) for those outside of Quebec. Heath says this change would mean fewer people would have to prepay their taxes.
 The new thresholds would apply to the 2028 tax year and would be indexed to inflation going forward.
 Offering optional flat-amount tax deductions and credits
 “Having to keep track of receipts throughout the year adds to the burden of complying with the tax system and can discourage Canadians from claiming the deductions and credits that they are eligible for,” the budget says. That’s why the government proposes introducing optional flat amounts for some deductions and credits starting in the 2027 tax year.
 People who move for work or school would be able to deduct an optional flat $1,000 under the Moving Expense Deduction (for costs such as travel, transporting or storing household items, and meals and temporary accommodation), with no receipts required. However, Heath points out that moving costs can require thousands to tens of thousands of dollars. “A lot of people will be better off documenting the actual amounts,” Heath says.
 The government also proposes a one-time optional flat expense amount of $1,000 for the Home Accessibility Tax Credit, which allows eligible individuals and supporting family members to claim up to $20,000 in qualifying home renovation or alteration expenses per year. This will be helpful for those who have incurred a lot of little costs, Pegler says. But for those who will spend well over $1,000 on accessible home updates, keeping receipts and an itemized list of expenses may be worth the time and effort. “The trade-off of doing the flat rate or keeping all the records is something people will want to think about,” Pegler says. Those who claim the flat amount would still be required to retain some documents that substantiate qualifying expenses.
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
 ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW 
 Another proposal is that Canadians with celiac disease would be able to claim an optional flat amount of $1,000 for incremental costs of gluten-free food. This measure would apply to the 2026 tax year and beyond. Currently, Pegler says, people with celiac need to keep a record of gluten-free purchases and compare the costs to the normal price for that type of food, and they can claim the difference. “That’s a lot of record-keeping,” he says. This measure would allow them to claim $1,000 without keeping piles of receipts.
 A new deadline for filing taxes
 Currently, most individuals are required to file their T1 income tax return and pay any balance owing by April 30. Self-employed individuals and their spouses or common-law partners have until June 15 to file their returns, but any balance owing must be paid by April 30.
 The budget proposes changing the filing and balance-due   dates to May 15 for everyone, including those who are self-employed and their spouses or common-law partners. This measure would apply for the 2027 tax year and beyond.
 According to the budget, this measure is expected to save taxpayers $230 million in interest and penalty payments over five years.
 The government says a second set of measures toward tax simplification will be announced in the Spring Economic Update in 2027.
